The problem can be solved by constructing a schedule using a difference matrix over modulo 10 arithmetic. We can represent each of the 40 golfers as a pair (r, x) where r ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3} and x ∈ {0, 1, ..., 9}. The golfer's index is p = r * 10 + x. For a given week w ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}, we assign golfer (r, x) to group g = (x + r * w) mod 10. 

To prove no pair of golfers meets more than once, suppose two distinct golfers (r1, x1) and (r2, x2) are in the same group in weeks w1 and w2. This implies:
x1 + r1 * w1 ≡ x2 + r2 * w1 (mod 10)
x1 + r1 * w2 ≡ x2 + r2 * w2 (mod 10)
Subtracting the two congruences yields (r1 - r2) * (w1 - w2) ≡ 0 (mod 10). Since r1, r2 ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}, the maximum absolute difference |r1 - r2| is 3. Similarly, the maximum absolute difference |w1 - w2| is 4. The product of these differences can be at most 12. The only multiple of 10 in the range [1, 12] is 10, which cannot be formed by multiplying any two integers from {1, 2, 3} and {1, 2, 3, 4}. Thus, the product can only be 0, meaning either r1 = r2 (which implies x1 = x2, so they are the same golfer) or w1 = w2 (they only meet in one week). This guarantees all constraints are perfectly satisfied.
